newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to end limits on foreigner T-bill trade.
newsitem.headline: Russia to end limits on foreigner T-bill trade.

text.p: Russia will end all restrictions on non-residents repatriating earnings from government securities from January 1, 1998, the Central Bank said on Friday.

"At its meeting on February 19 the Credit Committee of the Bank of Russia confirmed the timetable for gradual liberalisation of participation by non-residents in the government securities market," the bank said in a statement.

This involves the step-by-step removal during 1997 of the requirement on non-residents to conduct forward deals to repatriate their profits on Treasury bills and bonds, and the cap on the guaranteed dollar yield for non-residents, it said.

The bank noted that the removal of the limits would enable Russia to meet its obligations under Article Eight of the International Monetary Fund charter, which establishes rules for currency convertibility.
The full timetable will be approved by the bank's board of directors and published within the next two weeks, after being agreed with the Finance Ministry, it said.
Russia opened up the government securities market to foreigners last year, allowing them to open special rouble "S" accounts at designated Russian banks.
Funds in these accounts can be used to buy T-bills and bonds at auction or in the secondary market.
But funds can only be repatriated through forward or option deals.

The Central Bank also requires Russian banks to offset part of non-residents' rouble purchases and forward rouble sales with the central bank at non-market rates which it sets to determine the dollar return available to non-residents.
The Central Bank has been gradually reducing the required proportion of these compensatory deals, and the minimum tenor of the forward deals, as part of a committment to open up the market further.
It has also been cutting the guaranteed dollar yield, which is now 12.5 percent, compared with an average rouble yield in the market of around 30 percent.
The guaranteed dollar yield applies to investments held to maturity. But bond dealers say non-residents can earn much higher returns by trading aggressively in the secondary market.
